lab_title: The Mystery of Retrograde Motion: From Epicycles to Orbits
top_level_objectives: Observe and describe the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion for outer planets.
Explain apparent retrograde motion using the heliocentric model and relative orbital speeds.
Contrast the complexity of explaining retrograde motion in a geocentric model versus the elegance of the heliocentric explanation.
Compare the characteristics of retrograde motion for different outer planets like Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce students to the puzzling observation of Mars's apparent retrograde motion from Earth's perspective.
key_visuals: A realistic night sky projection with identifiable constellations.
Mars rendered as a reddish point of light.
A time-lapse path showing Mars's eastward drift, slowing, reversing westward in a loop, and then resuming eastward motion.
student_actions: Set the observation date and time.
Fast-forward through several weeks/months of time to observe Mars's path against the background stars.
Identify and trace the retrograde loop Mars makes in the sky.
Annotate the direction of Mars's motion (eastward/westward) at different points.

scenes.brief_purpose: To highlight why the observed retrograde motion presented a significant challenge to the ancient geocentric model of the universe.
key_visuals: A conceptual representation of the Earth at the center of the universe.
A simplified, conceptual depiction of Mars orbiting Earth.
Optional: A subtle, 'ghosted' representation of an epicycle suggesting the complexity required by the geocentric model to explain the observed motion.
student_actions: Review the observed retrograde path from the previous scene.
Consider how Mars's observed motion conflicts with a simple, direct orbit around Earth.
Reflect on the difficulties ancient astronomers faced in explaining this phenomenon.

scenes.brief_purpose: To establish the fundamental setup of the heliocentric model with the Sun, Earth, and Mars in their respective orbits.
key_visuals: A central Sun model emitting light.
An orbital path for Earth (closer to the Sun).
An orbital path for Mars (further from the Sun).
Labelled models of Earth and Mars.
student_actions: Place the Sun at the center of the AR space.
Position Earth's orbital plane and Earth model.
Position Mars's orbital plane and Mars model.
Verify the relative distances and orbital speeds (conceptual) of Earth and Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: To demonstrate how the relative orbital speeds of Earth and Mars in the heliocentric model naturally produce apparent retrograde motion.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model with the Sun, Earth, and Mars in motion along their orbits.
A projected line of sight from Earth through Mars to a distant background star field.
A trace of Mars's apparent position on the background star field as observed from Earth.
student_actions: Start the orbital simulation, observing Earth and Mars moving at their correct relative speeds.
Observe the line of sight from Earth to Mars as Earth overtakes Mars.
Identify the period when Mars appears to move 'backward' against the background stars.
Switch viewpoint to directly 'ride' on Earth and observe Mars's apparent path.

scenes.brief_purpose: To reinforce the concept of apparent retrograde motion using a relatable everyday analogy of one car passing another.
key_visuals: Two cars on parallel tracks, one moving faster than the other.
A static background object (e.g., a tree, distant building).
Arrows indicating the apparent motion of the slower car as viewed from the faster car while passing.
student_actions: Initiate the car simulation.
Observe the apparent motion of the slower car from the perspective of the faster car.
Relate this observed relative motion to the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as seen from Earth.
Adjust relative speeds of the cars to see how it affects the perceived motion.

scenes.scene_name: Comparing Retrograde Motion: Jupiter and Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: To compare the characteristics of apparent retrograde motion for different outer planets, noting the influence of orbital distance and relative speed.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model extended to include the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
Simultaneous or sequential simulations of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn's apparent retrograde loops.
Data overlays showing orbital periods and distances for each planet.
student_actions: Select and observe the retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Compare the 'size' or duration of the retrograde loops for each planet.
Analyze the relationship between a planet's orbital distance/speed and the prominence of its retrograde motion.
Discuss why more distant planets exhibit less dramatic retrograde motion.
